claim: Memory formation depends on neural activity across a network of regions, including the hippocampus and broader medial temporal lobe (MTL).
source: Memory formation depends on neural activity across a network of regions, including the hippocampus and broader medial temporal lobe (MTL).
evidence: This is a general statement about memory formation that draws from established scientific consensus in neuroscience.

claim: Extracellular spikes were recorded from 1854 single- and multi-units simultaneously with hippocampal local field potentials (LFPs) in 28 neurosurgical patients who completed virtual navigation experiments.
source: We recorded extracellular spikes from 1854 single- and multi-units simultaneously with hippocampal local field potentials (LFPs) in 28 neurosurgical patients who completed virtual navigation experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: A majority of hippocampal neurons phase-locked to oscillations in the slow (2–4 Hz) or fast (6–10 Hz) theta bands.
source: A majority of hippocampal neurons phase-locked to oscillations in the slow (2–4 Hz) or fast (6–10 Hz) theta bands, with a significant subset exhibiting nested slow theta × beta frequency (13–20 Hz) phase-locking.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A significant subset of hippocampal neurons exhibited nested slow theta × beta frequency (13–20 Hz) phase-locking.
source: A majority of hippocampal neurons phase-locked to oscillations in the slow (2–4 Hz) or fast (6–10 Hz) theta bands, with a significant subset exhibiting nested slow theta × beta frequency (13–20 Hz) phase-locking.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Outside of the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred only at theta frequencies.
source: Outside of the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred only at theta frequencies and primarily among neurons in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred primarily among neurons in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
source: Outside of the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred only at theta frequencies and primarily among neurons in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Extrahippocampal neurons phase-locked to hippocampal theta even when theta did not appear locally.
source: Moreover, extrahippocampal neurons phase-locked to hippocampal theta even when theta did not appear locally.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Spike-time synchronization with hippocampal theta is a defining feature of neuronal activity in the hippocampus and structurally connected MTL regions.
source: These results indicate that spike-time synchronization with hippocampal theta is a defining feature of neuronal activity in the hippocampus and structurally connected MTL regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Theta phase-locking could mediate flexible communication with the hippocampus to influence the content and quality of memories.
source: Theta phase-locking could mediate flexible communication with the hippocampus to influence the content and quality of memories.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functional role of theta phase-locking.

claim: The hippocampus is the operational hub of a spatially distributed episodic memory system that enables us to remember past experiences in rich detail, together with the place and time at which they occurred.
source: The hippocampus is the operational hub of a spatially distributed episodic memory system that enables us to remember past experiences in rich detail, together with the place and time at which they occurred (Eichenbaum, 2000; Moscovitch et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Theta (2–10 Hz) oscillations within the hippocampus facilitate interactions between the hippocampus and other brain regions.
source: A leading hypothesis is that theta (2–10 Hz) oscillations within the hippocampus facilitate interactions between the hippocampus and other brain regions (Buzsáki, 2010; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Moscovitch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal neurons are more receptive to synaptic excitation at specific theta phases.
source: Hippocampal neurons are more receptive to synaptic excitation at specific theta phases (Kamondi et al., 1998), so well-timed inputs can more effectively drive activity than inputs at random phases (Fries, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term potentiation and long-term depression in the rodent hippocampus depend on theta phase.
source: Long-term potentiation and long-term depression in the rodent hippocampus also depend on theta phase (Pavlides et al., 1988; Huerta and Lisman, 1995; Hyman et al., 2003), offering a possible link between the phase at which inputs arrive and the strength of their encoding.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: mPFC neurons phase-lock to hippocampal theta during short-term memory tasks.
source: mPFC neurons phase-lock to hippocampal theta during short-term memory tasks (Siapas et al., 2005; Hyman et al., 2005; Sirota et al., 2008), and stronger phase-locking predicts better performance (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Hyman et al., 2010; Benchenane et al., 2010; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011) and greater information transfer between mPFC and hippocampal neurons (Ito et al., 2018; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stronger phase-locking to hippocampal theta predicts better performance in memory tasks.
source: mPFC neurons phase-lock to hippocampal theta during short-term memory tasks (Siapas et al., 2005; Hyman et al., 2005; Sirota et al., 2008), and stronger phase-locking predicts better performance (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Hyman et al., 2010; Benchenane et al., 2010; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011) and greater information transfer between mPFC and hippocampal neurons (Ito et al., 2018; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phase-locking to hippocampal theta is prevalent among cells in the entorhinal cortex, amygdala, parietal cortex, thalamic nucleus reuniens, and some subcortical and brainstem nuclei.
source: Phase-locking to hippocampal theta is also prevalent among cells in many other regions, including the entorhinal cortex (EC), amygdala, parietal cortex, thalamic nucleus reuniens, and some subcortical and brainstem nuclei (Kocsis and Vertes, 1992; Sirota et al., 2008; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011; Bienvenu et al., 2012; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Theta phase-synchronization could be a general mechanism for relaying information between the hippocampus and a broad network of memory-related regions.
source: Theta phase-synchronization could thus be a general mechanism for relaying information between the hippocampus and a broad network of memory-related regions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from cited research.

claim: Macroelectrode LFP recordings in epilepsy patients have revealed sporadically occurring theta oscillations in the hippocampus and cortex during spatial navigation and episodic memory engagement.
source: In humans, macroelectrode LFP recordings in epilepsy patients have revealed sporadically occurring theta oscillations in the hippocampus and cortex during spatial navigation and episodic memory engagement (Ekstrom et al., 2005; Watrous et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012; Watrous et al., 2013a; Zhang and Jacobs, 2015; Vass et al., 2016; Aghajan et al., 2017; Stangl et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Macroscale theta phase-synchronization within the MTL and PFC has consistently correlated with better memory performance.
source: Macroscale theta phase-synchronization within the MTL and PFC has consistently correlated with better memory performance (Babiloni et al., 2009; Watrous et al., 2013b; Solomon et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019; Kunz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A large percentage of MTL and neocortical neurons phase-locked to locally recorded theta oscillations as subjects navigated through a virtual environment.
source: An early study in epilepsy patients found that a large percentage of MTL and neocortical neurons phase-locked to locally recorded theta oscillations (among other frequencies) as subjects navigated through a virtual environment (Jacobs et al., 2007), and another study found that MTL neurons phase-locked more strongly to locally recorded theta oscillations while subjects viewed images that they later recognized than those that they forgot (Rutishauser et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MTL neurons phase-locked more strongly to locally recorded theta oscillations while subjects viewed images that they later recognized than those that they forgot.
source: An early study in epilepsy patients found that a large percentage of MTL and neocortical neurons phase-locked to locally recorded theta oscillations (among other frequencies) as subjects navigated through a virtual environment (Jacobs et al., 2007), and another study found that MTL neurons phase-locked more strongly to locally recorded theta oscillations while subjects viewed images that they later recognized than those that they forgot (Rutishauser et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased coupling between spikes and distal theta oscillations in the MTL during an associative image encoding task predicted better subsequent recognition.
source: A recent study found that increased coupling between spikes and distal theta oscillations in the MTL during an associative image encoding task predicted better subsequent recognition (Roux et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Subjects were implanted with depth electrodes in the hippocampus, EC, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus (PHG), superior temporal gyrus (STG), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: Subjects were implanted with depth electrodes in the hippocampus, EC, amygdala, parahippocampal gyrus (PHG), superior temporal gyrus (STG), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and data collection methods.

claim: 10–71 neurons per session were identified across 55 recording sessions, with a median of 30.0 neurons.
source: In total, we identified 10–71 (median = 30.0) neurons per session across 55 recording sessions, and the firing rates of these neurons were log-normally distributed (median = 2.0 Hz).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: The firing rates of neurons were log-normally distributed with a median of 2.0 Hz.
source: In total, we identified 10–71 (median = 30.0) neurons per session across 55 recording sessions, and the firing rates of these neurons were log-normally distributed (median = 2.0 Hz).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Every subject had at least one microwire bundle implanted in the hippocampus.
source: In addition, every subject had at least one microwire bundle implanted in the hippocampus, permitting neuronal firing to be analyzed simultaneously with oscillatory activity in the hippocampal LFP.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Many individual hippocampal electrodes showed peaks in spectral power that rose above the background 1/f line in session-averaged LFP spectrograms.
source: Many individual electrodes showed peaks in spectral power that rose above the background 1/f line in session-averaged LFP spectrograms (Figure 1A), indicating the potential presence of oscillatory activity (Donoghue et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Spectral peaks in hippocampal LFPs appeared nearly exclusively between 2–20 Hz.
source: The frequency and magnitude of these spectral peaks varied considerably across subjects (compare Figure 1A subpanels) yet appeared nearly exclusively between 2–20 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Hippocampal oscillatory bouts were present approximately 1–6% of the time at the examined frequencies.
source: Across subjects, hippocampal oscillatory bouts were present ∼1–6% of the time at the examined frequencies (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows oscillatory prevalence in other regions for comparison).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The prevalence of hippocampal oscillations clustered around three, well-separated bands with peaks at 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz.
source: The prevalence of these oscillations was not uniform across frequencies, but instead clustered around three, well-separated bands with peaks at 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The observed oscillation frequencies are consistent with hippocampal slow theta (2–4 Hz), fast theta (6–10 Hz), and beta band rhythms (13–20 Hz) previously described in macroelectrode recordings.
source: These frequencies are consistent with the hippocampal slow theta (alternatively 'delta' 2–4 Hz), fast theta (6–10 Hz), and beta band rhythms (13–20 Hz) previously described in macroelectrode recordings, and the prevalence of oscillatory bouts in our data was comparable to these earlier studies (Ekstrom et al., 2005; Lega et al., 2012; Watrous et al., 2013a; Goyal et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research cited.

claim: Mean LFP waveforms during the first three cycles of each oscillatory bout showed symmetrical, sinusoidal shapes at each peak frequency, without any apparent harmonics.
source: Mean LFP waveforms during the first three cycles of each oscillatory bout showed symmetrical, sinusoidal shapes at each peak frequency, without any apparent harmonics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 3 Hz and 7 Hz oscillations were nearly perfectly symmetrical, while the 15 Hz oscillation showed a very small asymmetry associated with a longer (by <1 ms) ascending than descending period.
source: We computed an asymmetry index for each waveform and confirmed that, on average across subjects, the 3 Hz and 7 Hz oscillations were nearly perfectly symmetrical, while the 15 Hz oscillation showed a very small asymmetry associated with a longer (by <1 ms) ascending than descending period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz oscillations occurred at largely separable times.
source: We found that the 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz oscillations occurred at largely separable times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hippocampal oscillatory bouts occur in three independent bands, centered at 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz.
source: We concluded that hippocampal oscillatory bouts occur in three independent bands, centered at 3 Hz, 7 Hz, and 15 Hz.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The human hippocampus exhibits several distinct, low-frequency oscillations that are conserved across spatial scales spanning several orders of magnitude, from microwire to macroelectrode fields.
source: These findings indicate that the human hippocampus exhibits several distinct, low-frequency oscillations that are conserved across spatial scales spanning several orders of magnitude, from microwire to macroelectrode fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Theta oscillations are the predominant oscillatory component of the hippocampal LFP during virtual navigation.
source: Moreover, theta oscillations are the predominant oscillatory component of the hippocampal LFP during virtual navigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 59% of hippocampal neurons significantly phase-locked to hippocampal oscillations after FDR correction.
source: As expected, neurons within the hippocampus phase-locked to hippocampal oscillations at the highest rate among recorded regions, with 59% of hippocampal neurons significantly phase-locked after FDR correction.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Phase-locking to the hippocampus occurred at rates below 5% in PHG, STG, OFC, and ACC.
source: These results stood in stark contrast to all remaining regions, where phase-locking to the hippocampus occurred at rates below 5%.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Phase-locking to local oscillations was prevalent in the PHG (24%) and STG (49%).
source: Phase-locking to local oscillations was nonetheless prevalent in the PHG (24%) and STG (49%), indicating that many of these neurons fired at specific phases of LFP oscillations — just not those recorded in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The hippocampus, EC, and amygdala feature strong spike-time synchronization to hippocampal oscillations.
source: Altogether, these results highlight a triad of regions — the hippocampus, EC, and amygdala — that features strong spike-time synchronization to hippocampal oscillations, while neurons in more remote, cortical regions that are known to interact with hippocampus-dependent processes (Eichenbaum, 2000; Squire, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012) phase-locked minimally to hippocampal rhythms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Neurons in more remote, cortical regions phase-locked minimally to hippocampal rhythms.
source: Altogether, these results highlight a triad of regions — the hippocampus, EC, and amygdala — that features strong spike-time synchronization to hippocampal oscillations, while neurons in more remote, cortical regions that are known to interact with hippocampus-dependent processes (Eichenbaum, 2000; Squire, 2011; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012) phase-locked minimally to hippocampal rhythms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: In the hippocampus, neurons phase-locked to local oscillations predominantly between 2–20 Hz.
source: In the hippocampus, neurons phase-locked to local oscillations predominantly between 2–20 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Within the 2–20 Hz range, hippocampal neuron phase-locking clustered around three distinct peaks in the slow theta, fast theta, and beta bands.
source: Within the 2–20 Hz range, phase-locking was not unimodal, but instead clustered around three distinct peaks in the slow theta, fast theta, and beta bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Most hippocampal neurons phase-locked only to a single band, with the exception of neurons that phase-locked maximally to beta oscillations, which also showed a near-universal tendency to phase-lock strongly to slow theta.
source: Most hippocampal neurons phase-locked only to a single band, with the exception of neurons that phase-locked maximally to beta oscillations, which also showed a near-universal tendency to phase-lock strongly to slow theta (see for example Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: Nested slow theta × beta phase-locking neurons have not previously been reported.
source: These neurons may best be classified as nested slow theta × beta phase-locking neurons, which to our knowledge have not previously been reported.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Nested phase-locking between fast theta and beta oscillations or between any other pair of frequency bands was not observed.
source: In contrast, we did not observe nested phase-locking between fast theta and beta oscillations or between any other pair of frequency bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Among neurons outside the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred within a more constrained frequency range, between 2–10 Hz.
source: Among neurons outside the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurred within a more constrained frequency range, between 2–10 Hz (Figure 3B, right three subpanels).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: In the EC, similar numbers of neurons showed preferential phase-locking to slow and fast hippocampal theta.
source: In the EC, similar numbers of neurons showed preferential phase-locking to slow and fast hippocampal theta, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: In the amygdala and remaining cortical regions, only a few neurons phase-locked to fast hippocampal theta, while most neurons coupled exclusively to slow theta.
source: In the amygdala and remaining cortical regions, this balance shifted: Only a few neurons phase-locked to fast hippocampal theta, while most neurons coupled exclusively to slow theta.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: For neurons outside the hippocampus, spike-time synchronization with hippocampal oscillations was restricted to theta frequencies.
source: Thus, while hippocampal neurons phase-locked to both theta and beta bands, for neurons outside the hippocampus, spike-time synchronization with hippocampal oscillations was restricted to theta frequencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Hippocampal oscillations overlapped more with oscillations in the EC and amygdala than with oscillations in the STG, OFC, and ACC at most frequencies.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, hippocampal oscillations overlapped more with oscillations in the EC and amygdala than with oscillations in the STG, OFC, and ACC at most frequencies (Figure 4A; overlap calculated using the Dice similarity coefficient).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The overlap between local and hippocampal oscillations never exceeded 20% in any region at any frequency.
source: Moreover, the overlap between local and hippocampal oscillations never exceeded 20% in any region at any frequency, indicating that neurons could, in principle, phase-lock to hippocampal oscillations independent of local oscillations, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: When hippocampal oscillations occurred without co-occurring local oscillations, phase-locking rates to the hippocampus declined by nearly two-thirds in the EC (from 39% to 14% of neurons) and by half in the amygdala (from 28% to 15%).
source: In contrast, when hippocampal oscillations occurred without co-occurring local oscillations, phase-locking rates to the hippocampus declined by nearly two-thirds in the EC (from 39% to 14% of neurons) and by half in the amygdala (from 28% to 15%), while phase-locking to the hippocampus in other regions mostly vanished.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Phase-locking strength to the hippocampus decreased specifically at theta frequencies when local oscillations were absent.
source: Phase-locking strength to the hippocampus decreased specifically at theta frequencies, and even neurons that remained significantly phase-locked in the absence of local oscillations showed reduced phase-locking strength (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: In the EC, the percentage of locally phase-locked neurons was reduced by more than half when hippocampal oscillations were absent.
source: While hippocampal oscillation presence did not affect local phase-locking rates in the amygdala and neocortex, in the EC the percentage of locally phase-locked neurons was reduced by more than half when hippocampal oscillations were absent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: When local theta was absent, the strength of EC and amygdala neuron phase-locking to hippocampal theta was reduced by half, while still remaining well above chance.
source: When local theta was absent, the strength of EC and amygdala neuron phase-locking to hippocampal theta was reduced by half, while still remaining well above chance (Figure 4D, right subpanel).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Interregional LFP–LFP theta coupling augments but is not strictly required for extrahippocampal neuron phase-locking to hippocampal theta.
source: Collectively, these results provide direct evidence that interregional LFP–LFP theta coupling augments but is not strictly required for extrahippocampal neuron phase-locking to hippocampal theta.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Individual hippocampal neurons phase-lock to oscillations in slow theta, fast theta, and beta bands.
source: Consistent with prior studies, we identify sporadic, oscillatory bouts in hippocampal LFPs within slow theta (2–4 Hz), fast theta (6–10 Hz), and beta (13–20 Hz) bands while subjects engaged in virtual navigation. Individual hippocampal neurons phase-lock to oscillations in each of these bands, including a previously undiscovered group of neurons that phase-lock to nested slow theta and beta rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A previously undiscovered group of neurons phase-lock to nested slow theta and beta rhythms.
source: Consistent with prior studies, we identify sporadic, oscillatory bouts in hippocampal LFPs within slow theta (2–4 Hz), fast theta (6–10 Hz), and beta (13–20 Hz) bands while subjects engaged in virtual navigation. Individual hippocampal neurons phase-lock to oscillations in each of these bands, including a previously undiscovered group of neurons that phase-lock to nested slow theta and beta rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Outside the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurs in both a region-specific (primarily EC and amygdala neurons) and frequency-specific (theta-preferring) manner.
source: Outside the hippocampus, phase-locking to hippocampal oscillations occurs in both a region-specific (primarily EC and amygdala neurons) and frequency-specific (theta-preferring) manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There is a dissociation between region and frequency in the selective phase-locking of EC neurons to fast hippocampal theta, whereas neurons in all regions outside the hippocampus show some level of phase-locking to slow hippocampal theta.
source: We further show a dissociation between region and frequency in the selective phase-locking of EC neurons to fast hippocampal theta, whereas neurons in all regions outside the hippocampus show some level of phase-locking to slow hippocampal theta.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Extrahippocampal neurons phase-lock approximately twice as strongly to hippocampal theta when local theta oscillations co-occur, as when local theta is absent.
source: Finally, we provide the first direct evidence in humans that LFP–LFP coupling enhances spike-time synchronization between regions, as extrahippocampal neurons phase-lock approximately twice as strongly to hippocampal theta when local theta oscillations co-occur, as when local theta is absent.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There is a fundamental relationship between MTL neuron firing and hippocampal theta phase.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal a fundamental relationship between MTL neuron firing and hippocampal theta phase that underscores a hypothesized role for theta oscillations in routing the information contents of memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The hippocampus maintains strong, reciprocal connections with the EC and amygdala while connections to neocortex are sparser.
source: This result is consistent with structural anatomy, as the hippocampus maintains strong, reciprocal connections with the EC and amygdala while connections to neocortex are sparser (Amaral, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some mPFC neurons project directly to the hippocampus.
source: Still, given evidence in rodents that some mPFC neurons project directly to the hippocampus (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015), phase-lock to hippocampal theta (Siapas et al., 2005; Hyman et al., 2005; Sirota et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2018; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019), and are critical for memory retrieval (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015; Yadav et al., 2022), we expected ACC and OFC neurons to show stronger associations with hippocampal theta than we observed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: mPFC neurons are critical for memory retrieval.
source: Still, given evidence in rodents that some mPFC neurons project directly to the hippocampus (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015), phase-lock to hippocampal theta (Siapas et al., 2005; Hyman et al., 2005; Sirota et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2018; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019), and are critical for memory retrieval (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015; Yadav et al., 2022), we expected ACC and OFC neurons to show stronger associations with hippocampal theta than we observed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Strong phase-locking to hippocampal theta may occur in the EC and amygdala at baseline, whereas phase-locking among neurons in the mPFC and other cortical areas may be task-dependent.
source: One possibility is that strong phase-locking to hippocampal theta occurs in the EC and amygdala at baseline, whereas phase-locking among neurons in the mPFC and other cortical areas is task-dependent.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for the findings.

claim: ACC and pre-supplementary motor area neurons phase-locked to hippocampal theta during a task-switching experiment in which subjects alternated between making recognition memory-based or categorization-based decisions.
source: Consistently, a recent study in humans found that ACC and pre-supplementary motor area neurons phase-locked to hippocampal theta during a task-switching experiment in which subjects alternated between making recognition memory-based or categorization-based decisions (Minxha et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Amygdala neurons phase-lock at higher rates to local than to hippocampal oscillations, and local and hippocampal phase-locking occur at least somewhat independently.
source: First, as in neocortical regions, amygdala neurons phase-lock at higher rates to local than to hippocampal oscillations, and local and hippocampal phase-locking occur at least somewhat independently.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: EC neurons phase-lock to local and hippocampal theta oscillations at indistinguishable rates, and phase-locking is greatly disrupted when EC and hippocampal theta bouts are asynchronous.
source: By contrast, EC neurons phase-lock to local and hippocampal theta oscillations at indistinguishable rates, and phase-locking is greatly disrupted when EC and hippocampal theta bouts are asynchronous.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the experimental data analysis.

claim: In rodents, EC and hippocampal theta are phase-shifted but otherwise largely interchangeable, with EC inputs playing a major role in hippocampal theta generation.
source: It is worth noting that in rodents, EC and hippocampal theta are phase-shifted but otherwise largely interchangeable, with EC inputs playing a major role in hippocampal theta generation (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Theta phase-synchronization between EC and hippocampus is critical in explaining many circuit-level phenomena in rodents, including grid cell and place cell interactions, phase precession, and encoding/retrieval phase separation.
source: Theta phase-synchronization between these regions is critical in explaining many circuit-level phenomena in rodents, including grid cell and place cell interactions, phase precession, and encoding/retrieval phase separation (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; Hasselmo, 2005; Burgess et al., 2007; Bonnevie et al., 2013; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Theta occurs more sporadically in humans and other primates than in rodents.
source: Theta occurs more sporadically in humans and other primates than in rodents, and may differ between mammals in other ways not yet well understood (Eliav et al., 2018; Trimper and Colgin, 2018; Bush and Burgess, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EC and hippocampal neurons in humans retain a uniquely high degree of spike-time synchronization with an overlapping theta rhythm.
source: Still, our results indicate that as in rodents, EC and hippocampal neurons in humans retain a uniquely high degree of spike-time synchronization with an overlapping theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Hippocampal theta frequency varies along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus, with faster theta occurring more posteriorly.
source: This result may be placed in context with recent observations that hippocampal theta frequency varies along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus, with faster theta occurring more posteriorly (Goyal et al., 2020; Penner et al., 2022), where the density of EC relative to amygdalar afferents is greater (Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The density of EC relative to amygdalar afferents is greater in the posterior hippocampus.
source: This result may be placed in context with recent observations that hippocampal theta frequency varies along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus, with faster theta occurring more posteriorly (Goyal et al., 2020; Penner et al., 2022), where the density of EC relative to amygdalar afferents is greater (Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All subjects had pharmacoresistant epilepsy.
source: First, all subjects had pharmacoresistant epilepsy, and we cannot rule out that some results might stem from pathological activity.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study related to the subject population.

claim: Subjects were 28 patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who were implanted with depth electrodes to monitor seizure activity.
source: Subjects were 28patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who were implanted with depth electrodes to monitor seizure activity.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Subjects completed one of two experiments: Yellow Cab (18 subjects) or Goldmine (10 subjects).
source: Subjects completed one of two experiments (see 'Spatial navigation tasks'): Yellow Cab (18 subjects) or Goldmine (10 subjects).
evidence: This describes the experimental tasks used in the study.

claim: Data were analyzed from 55 recording sessions (1–4 sessions per subject, mean duration = 33.6 min).
source: We analyzed data from 55 recording sessions (1–4 sessions per subject, mean duration = 33.6 min).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Each subject was implanted with 6–12 Behnke-Fried depth electrodes that feature macroelectrode contacts for clinical monitoring and 40 µm–diameter, platinum-iridium microwires for measuring microscale LFPs and extracellular action potentials.
source: Each subject was implanted with 6–12 Behnke-Fried depth electrodes that feature macroelectrode contacts for clinical monitoring and 40 µm–diameter, platinum-iridium microwires for measuring microscale LFPs and extracellular action potentials (Fried et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the recording equipment used in the study.

claim: Microwire LFPs were amplified and sampled at 28–32 kHz on a Neuralynx Cheetah or Blackrock NeuroPort recording system.
source: Microwire LFPs were amplified and sampled at 28–32 kHz on a Neuralynx Cheetah (Neuralynx, Tucson, AZ) or Blackrock NeuroPort (Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT) recording system.
evidence: This describes the recording equipment and parameters used in the study.
